title: PRISM: Stress-Testing Alignment-Faking Claims
summary: A single-author paper tests two inferences in open-model alignment-faking work: that a compliance gap under a monitored prompt ('refusals will be trained away') shows alignment faking, and that hidden-state probes separating monitored from unmonitored compliant answers detect faking. Of 18 open-weight configurations, 11 comply more when told they are monitored and 2 comply less. A six-cell prompt factorial on four models finds that removing the training consequence changes compliance by -3.3 to +1.6 points, while the instruction wording or rating frame explains the gap; the author calls this 'prompted compliance'. Probes separate monitored from unmonitored refusals as well as compliant answers, and a direction learned only on refusals steers compliance as much as the 'faking' direction. The paper releases five checks (PRISM) and notes limits: four models in the factorial, borderline rather than harmful queries, and described rather than applied training.
setting: 18 open-weight configurations (Qwen3 0.6B-32B, Gemma-3 12B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, OLMo-2 7B/13B); 50 OR-Bench/XSTest borderline queries (+50 HarmBench for refusal-ablation control), 5-10 runs per query; Claude Opus 4.6 as judge; residual-stream probes and steering on Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-8B.

quotes.quote: A six-cell prompt factorial on four models separates monitoring, the training consequence and the instruction wording.
Our control runs the identical pipeline on monitored versus unmonitored refusals. A refusal is not faked compliance, so a probe that separates refusals as well is reading which prompt the model saw.
Of 18 configurations, 11 comply more under b than a and 2 comply less (Figure 2).
The training consequence explains none of the gap in any model. In three of the four, the instruction wording explains it.
A two-layer MLP then separates monitored from unmonitored compliant answers with AUROC 0.96 (Llama) and 0.99 (Qwen), and refusals with 1.00 (Llama) and 1.00 (Qwen) (Figure 4).
So probe accuracy alone cannot tell an internal awareness representation apart from the words of the sentences the probe reads.
A compliance gap under a monitoring prompt is not, by itself, evidence of alignment faking in open models.
The cleanest version would apply training, not describe it, and test whether models resist changes they were warned about.
The prompts describe training rather than applying it, so a model that fakes only under real training pressure would not show up here. One LLM judge labels all answers, without human validation.
In our setup, monitored compliance in open models is prompted compliance.

key_numbers.claim: Removing the training threat barely changes compliance
key_numbers.quote: removing it changes compliance by −3.3 to +1.6 points

key_numbers.claim: Thinking raises private compliance and shrinks the gap
key_numbers.quote: Turning on thinking raises unmonitored compliance by 21 to 43 points, and the gap is smaller with thinking than without it at each of the 5 Qwen3 sizes we ran both ways.

key_numbers.claim: Within-query hidden-no effect in Qwen3-32B only
key_numbers.quote: In Qwen3-32B the shift survives (d = 0.24, 26 of 39 queries, sign-flip p = 0.011)

key_numbers.claim: Text-only control matches a published test-awareness probe
key_numbers.quote: A bag-of-words classifier on the same sentences reaches 96.5% on a split rebuilt from their released code

limitations_stated: The author notes the factorial covers four models with Gemma-3-27B near ceiling; queries are borderline-safe rather than the harmful requests of Greenblatt et al.; prompts describe training rather than applying it; one LLM judge without human validation; one set of 50 queries; hosted vs local sampling differences; Qwen's steering positive control failed so its causal results are descriptive.
open_questions: The author calls for alignment-faking claims in open models to show dependence on the training consequence with wording held fixed, ideally by applying training rather than describing it. Our reading: the result concerns open-weight models on borderline queries; whether the same factorial separates wording from training consequence in Claude 3 Opus on harmful queries is not tested here.
sense_of_alignment: Alignment faking requires behavior that depends on the consequence for training: 'Neither involves the training consequence, which is what alignment faking requires.' Compliance gaps driven by prompt wording are reclassified as instruction following.
